Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23) | map = {{Infobox mapframe|type=shape|zoom=15|frame-width=200}} }} '''Takachiho Shrine''' (たかちほじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} located in [[Takachiho Town]], [[Nishiusuki District]], {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. It is a notable contender for the national historical shrine "Takachiho-Sume-Gami," though it was classified only as a village shrine under the modern shrine Ranking system. It is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the jurisdiction of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Shrine name == Historically, the shrine was known as "Jussha Daijingu" or "Jussha-no-Miya." In {{ill|1871|en|1871|WD=Q7746|lt=1871}} (4th year of [[Meiji]]), it was renamed "Mitai Shrine," and in {{ill|1895|en|1895|WD=Q7844|lt=1895}} (28th year of Meiji), it was renamed to its current name, Takachiho Shrine. == Deities == The primary deity enshrined is Takachiho-Sume-Gami in the first hall, and Jussha-Daijingu in the second hall. Takachiho-Sume-Gami refers collectively to the ancestral deities of Japanese mythology known as the "Three Generations of Hyuga" and their consorts (Amatsuhikohikohohodemi-no-Mikoto and Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto, Hoori-no-Mikoto and Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto, Hiko-nagisatake-ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto and Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto). Jussha-Daijingu refers to the elder brother of Emperor Jimmu, Mikenu-no-Mikoto, and nine other deities who are his wife and children (Unomehime-no-Mikoto and their children Mikotaro-no-Mikoto, Jiro-no-Mikoto, Saburo-no-Mikoto, Unemi-no-Mikoto, Teruno-no-Mikoto, Otono-no-Mikoto, Reisha-no-Mikoto, Asarabe-no-Mikoto). Mikenu-no-Mikoto, central to Jussha-Daijingu, is said to have crossed to the eternal land after stepping on the waves in the "Kojiki" and "Nihon Shoki," but local legend holds that he returned to Takachiho, vanquished the demon Kihachi, and established his palace here. The shrine's origin legend, "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki," dated March of the 5th year of Bunji (1189), states that Prince Masakazu, a son of Emperor Jimmu, defeated a demon called Kihachibushi, and later he and his descendants were enshrined as Jussha-Daijingu. Another legend in the "Hachiman Usa-gun Otogami-shu" of 1313 claims that Takachiho-Gami is another name for Kami-Yatsui-no-Mikoto, a child of Emperor Jimmu, and the elder brother of the deity enshrined at [[Aso Shrine]]. The "Heike Monogatari" describes Takachiho-Gami as a dragon revered in Hyūga Province. Unomehime-no-Mikoto, according to local legend, was rescued by Mikenu-no-Mikoto from the demon Kihachi and later became his consort. == History == Takachiho is traditionally known as the location of the Takachiho Palace, home to the "Three Generations of Hyuga" deities. The shrine incorporates elements of local beliefs, myths of the descent of deities, and [[Kumano Shugendo]] practices. The {{ill|Kushifuru Shrine|en|Kushifuru Shrine|WD=Q3200650|lt=Kushifuru Shrine}} has historically held autumn festivals in conjunction with the spring festivals of Takachiho Shrine. According to shrine legend, the shrine was established by Mikenu-no-Mikoto, who erected a sacred pole and enshrined the "Three Generations of Hyuga" deities and their consorts. Later, he and nine other deities were enshrined as Jussha-Daijingu. During the reign of Emperor Sujin, the first shrine buildings were constructed. If the shrine is indeed the historical "Takachiho-Gami," it received imperial recognition and Ranks, but it is not listed in the "Engishiki Jinmyōchō." During the mid-{{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, descendants of Mikenu-no-Mikoto served the shrine, and by the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}, it was revered by local lords and the imperial court. The shrine was associated with the Kumano shrines and played a significant role in local politics and religious practices. In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the shrine received 200 koku from the lords of the {{ill|Nobeoka Domain|en|Nobeoka Domain|WD=Q10863441|lt=Nobeoka Domain}}, and it was further supported by the {{ill|Miura|en|Miura|WD=Q347335|lt=Miura}} and [[Naito]] families. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], it was designated as a village shrine and later became a Beppyo Shrine in {{ill|1971|en|1971|WD=Q2475|lt=1971}} (46th year of {{ill|Shōwa|en|Shōwa|WD=Q398996|lt=Shōwa}}). === Ranks === As a historical shrine, it received Ranks such as Jugoi-ge in {{ill|843|en|843|WD=Q23469|lt=843}} and Jushii-jo in {{ill|858|en|858|WD=Q30371|lt=858}}. == ceremony == * **festival (April 16)** - Prayers for a good harvest, with a mikoshi procession to the Otabisho at [[Takamagahara Shrine]], where kagura is performed. * **Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23)** - All 33 dances of the Takachiho Night Kagura, designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property, are performed overnight. Throughout the year, a selection of four dances is performed for tourists. * **Inoshishi Kake Matsuri (December 3 of the lunar calendar)** - Originally a ritual involving the sacrifice of a 16-year-old virgin to appease the demon Kihachi, it was changed to the offering of wild boars by Kai Munekane, a retainer of the Mitai family. The ceremony includes offerings at the three Kihachi Kofuns and the Sasa Furi ceremony at the shrine, where a whole boar is offered, and the "Onihachinenase Uta" is sung while performing the "Sasa Furi Kagura." === Shrine Priests === According to the "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki," descendants of Jussha-Daijingu served as priests for generations. In 1314, a priest named Sone wrote about his family's long service to the shrine. The "Senmyo" priestly roles were established in the medieval period by the Mitai family, who divided the shrine's territory into ten districts, each served by a "Senmyo" priest. The roles and lineage of these priests remain unclear in later periods. == Shrine Buildings == The main hall is a large Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style building with a copper roof, featuring unique carvings related to local legends and rituals, such as the demon-slaying Mikenuno-no-Mikoto. The shrine is designated as an Important Cultural Property. In 1837, Matsuura Takeshiro described the shrine in his travel journal. == Sub-Shrines == * **Inari Shrine** - A small shrine attached to the east side of the main hall, dedicated to Kotoshironushi-no-Kami and Ootonoshi-no-Kami. * **Aratate Shrine and Shiko Shrine** - Located to the left of the main hall, dedicated to Sarutahiko-no-Mikoto, Amenouzume-no-Mikoto, Emperor Jimmu, and other imperial family members. The original Aratate Shrine was merged into Takachiho Shrine in the late Meiji period but was later reestablished at its original location. * **Other Sub-Shrines** - Gate Guardian deity (deity unknown), Yasaka Shrine (Susanoo-no-Mikoto), Goryo Shrine (Onakatomi-no-Mikoto), Tenjin Shrine (Sugawara-no-Michizane), Hibarino Shrine (Amanootomaro-no-Mikoto), Chinjusha (deity unknown), and the detached Ichi-no Shrine. == Cultural Properties == [[File:Takachiho-jinja, Hon-den 01.jpg|thumb|200px|main hall (Important Cultural Property)]] [[File:Takachiho-jinja, Sculpture Decoration of Hon-den 01.jpg|thumb|200px|Carvings on the main hall
Depicting the slaying of the demon Kihachi by Mikenuno-no-Mikoto.]] === National Important Cultural Property === * **main hall** - Built in 1778 in the early Edo period, featuring Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style with copper roofing, including an Inari shrine. The structure is noted for its detailed carvings and regional characteristics. Designated in 2004. * **Iron Komainu Pair** - Cast iron statues of guardian dogs donated by Minamoto no Yoritomo, designated in 1971. * **Wooden God Statues (2 sitting figures)** - Originally from Aratate Shrine, these statues were moved to Takachiho Shrine. They were designated as Important Cultural Property in 2020. === Takachiho Town Cultural Property === * **Nine God Masks** - Designated as Tangible Cultural Property in 1969. * **Takachiho Shrine Documents** - Designated as Tangible Cultural Property, including the "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki." * **Takachiho Shrine's Father Cedar** - A large cedar tree believed to have been planted by Hatakeyama Shigetada, designated as a Natural Monument in 1969. == Surrounding Historical Sites == * [[Takachiho Gorge]] * **Jussha-Daijingu Ichino-Shomori** - Town-designated historical site located in front of the shrine. * **Kihachi Mounds** - Three Kofuns for the demon Kihachi, located in Kamidono, Tokugenji Temple, and Takachiho High School. Other related sites include "Kihachi's Power Stone" in Takachiho Gorge, "Kihachi's Severed Stone" in Kamiyama, and "Kihachi's Knee Stone" in Take-no-sako. == References == {{Reflist}} == Further Reading == * Kenichi Tanigawa, ed. "Nihon no Kamigami - Shrines and Sacred Places" Volume 1, Kyushu, Hakusuisha, 1984 ISBN 4-560-02211-9 * "Miyazaki Prefecture's Place names" (Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei 46), Heibonsha, 1997 ISBN 4-582-49046-8 * "Udo Shrine and Takachiho Shrine" (Weekly Shrine Travel No. 47), Gakken, 2003 == Related Books == * S. Azu and Y. Umeda, eds., "Shinto Dictionary," Jinja Shinpōsha, 1968, pp. 35-36 * E. Shirai and M. Toki, eds., "Shrine Dictionary," Tōkyōdō Shuppan, 1979, p. 208 * M. Sugata, "Encyclopedia of Japanese Shrines," Nihon Bungeisha, 1989, pp. 238-239 * "The Book of Shinto," Gakken, 1992, p. 226 == See Also == {{Commonscat|Takachiho-jinja}} * {{ill|Kushifuru Shrine|en|Kushifuru Shrine|WD=Q3200650|lt=Kushifuru Shrine}} - Another contender for "Takachiho-Gami" == External Links == * [http://www.town-takachiho.jp/culture/tourism/post_81.html Takachiho Shrine] (Takachiho Town Office) * [http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/640101.html Takachiho Shrine] (Kokugakuin University) * [https://web.archive.org/web/20120530200534/http://kumaya.jp/atikoti43.html Takachiho Shrine] (Kumaya) * [http://www.komisen.net/index.htm Takachiho Town Community Center (Historical and Folk Museum)] {{Shinto Horizontal}} ==Admission fees== The shrine is open to the public. However, an admission fee is payable. *500 yen per person over 20 years old. *400 yen per person under 20 years old. ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Beppyo Shrines}}]] {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{translated page|ja|高千穂神社|version=103557806|comment=Imported full ja history}} [[image:takachihojinja.jpg|thumb|200px|Kagura Hall where nightly performances of Takachiho Night Kagura are held]] [[image:yokagura.jpg|thumb|200px|Night Kagura at the Kagura Hall]] [[en:Takachiho Shrine]] [[ja:高千穂神社]] {{Commons category|Takachiho-jinja}} [[fr:Takachiho-jinja]] [[zh:高千穗神社]] {{Commons category|Takachiho-jinja}} [[fr:Takachiho-jinja]] [[zh:高千穗神社]] {{wikidata link|Q3514126}} [[Category:Architecture of Takachiho Town]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Cultural heritage monuments in Japan]] [[Category:Edo period architecture]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties (buildings)]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:Important Cultural Property of Japan in Miyazaki prefecture]] [[Category:Kokushi genzaisha]] [[Category:Municipal History of Takachiho]] [[Category:Nobeoka Domain]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Hyūga Province]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Miyazaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Son-sha in Miyazaki Prefecture]] [[Category:translated pages with valid en interwikis]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Pages with unclosed square brackets]]

In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the shrine received 200 koku from the lords of the {{ill|Nobeoka Domain|en|Nobeoka Domain|WD=Q10863441|lt=Nobeoka Domain}}, and it was further supported by the {{ill|Miura|en|Miura|WD=Q347335|lt=Miura}} and [[Naito]] families. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], it was designated as a village shrine and later became a Beppyo Shrine in {{ill|1971|en|1971|WD=Q2475|lt=1971}} (46th year of {{ill|Shōwa|en|Shōwa|WD=Q398996|lt=Shōwa}}). === Ranks === As a historical shrine, it received Ranks such as Jugoi-ge in {{ill|843|en|843|WD=Q23469|lt=843}} and Jushii-jo in {{ill|858|en|858|WD=Q30371|lt=858}}. == ceremony == * **festival (April 16)** - Prayers for a good harvest, with a mikoshi procession to the Otabisho at [[Takamagahara Shrine]], where kagura is performed. * **Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23)** - All 33 dances of the Takachiho Night Kagura, designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property, are performed overnight. Throughout the year, a selection of four dances is performed for tourists. * **Inoshishi Kake Matsuri (December 3 of the lunar calendar)** - Originally a ritual involving the sacrifice of a 16-year-old virgin to appease the demon Kihachi, it was changed to the offering of wild boars by Kai Munekane, a retainer of the Mitai family. The ceremony includes offerings at the three Kihachi Kofuns and the Sasa Furi ceremony at the shrine, where a whole boar is offered, and the "Onihachinenase Uta" is sung while performing the "Sasa Furi Kagura." === Shrine Priests === According to the "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki," descendants of Jussha-Daijingu served as priests for generations. In 1314, a priest named Sone wrote about his family's long service to the shrine. The "Senmyo" priestly roles were established in the medieval period by the Mitai family, who divided the shrine's territory into ten districts, each served by a "Senmyo" priest. The roles and lineage of these priests remain unclear in later periods. == Shrine Buildings == The main hall is a large Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style building with a copper roof, featuring unique carvings related to local legends and rituals, such as the demon-slaying Mikenuno-no-Mikoto. The shrine is designated as an Important Cultural Property. In 1837, Matsuura Takeshiro described the shrine in his travel journal. == Sub-Shrines == * **Inari Shrine** - A small shrine attached to the east side of the main hall, dedicated to Kotoshironushi-no-Kami and Ootonoshi-no-Kami. * **Aratate Shrine and Shiko Shrine** - Located to the left of the main hall, dedicated to Sarutahiko-no-Mikoto, Amenouzume-no-Mikoto, Emperor Jimmu, and other imperial family members. The original Aratate Shrine was merged into Takachiho Shrine in the late Meiji period but was later reestablished at its original location. * **Other Sub-Shrines** - Gate Guardian deity (deity unknown), Yasaka Shrine (Susanoo-no-Mikoto), Goryo Shrine (Onakatomi-no-Mikoto), Tenjin Shrine (Sugawara-no-Michizane), Hibarino Shrine (Amanootomaro-no-Mikoto), Chinjusha (deity unknown), and the detached Ichi-no Shrine. == Cultural Properties == [[File:Takachiho-jinja, Hon-den 01.jpg|thumb|200px|main hall (Important Cultural Property)]] [[File:Takachiho-jinja, Sculpture Decoration of Hon-den 01.jpg|thumb|200px|Carvings on the main hall
Depicting the slaying of the demon Kihachi by Mikenuno-no-Mikoto.]] === National Important Cultural Property === * **main hall** - Built in 1778 in the early Edo period, featuring Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style with copper roofing, including an Inari shrine. The structure is noted for its detailed carvings and regional characteristics. Designated in 2004. * **Iron Komainu Pair** - Cast iron statues of guardian dogs donated by Minamoto no Yoritomo, designated in 1971. * **Wooden God Statues (2 sitting figures)** - Originally from Aratate Shrine, these statues were moved to Takachiho Shrine. They were designated as Important Cultural Property in 2020. === Takachiho Town Cultural Property === * **Nine God Masks** - Designated as Tangible Cultural Property in 1969. * **Takachiho Shrine Documents** - Designated as Tangible Cultural Property, including the "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki." * **Takachiho Shrine's Father Cedar** - A large cedar tree believed to have been planted by Hatakeyama Shigetada, designated as a Natural Monument in 1969. == Surrounding Historical Sites == * [[Takachiho Gorge]] * **Jussha-Daijingu Ichino-Shomori** - Town-designated historical site located in front of the shrine. * **Kihachi Mounds** - Three Kofuns for the demon Kihachi, located in Kamidono, Tokugenji Temple, and Takachiho High School. Other related sites include "Kihachi's Power Stone" in Takachiho Gorge, "Kihachi's Severed Stone" in Kamiyama, and "Kihachi's Knee Stone" in Take-no-sako. == References == {{Reflist}} == Further Reading == * Kenichi Tanigawa, ed. Azu and Y. Umeda, eds., "Shinto Dictionary," Jinja Shinpōsha, 1968, pp. 35-36 * E. Shirai and M. Toki, eds., "Shrine Dictionary," Tōkyōdō Shuppan, 1979, p. 208 * M. Sugata, "Encyclopedia of Japanese Shrines," Nihon Bungeisha, 1989, pp. 238-239 * "The Book of Shinto," Gakken, 1992, p. 226 == See Also == {{Commonscat|Takachiho-jinja}} * {{ill|Kushifuru Shrine|en|Kushifuru Shrine|WD=Q3200650|lt=Kushifuru Shrine}} - Another contender for "Takachiho-Gami" == External Links == * [http://www.town-takachiho.jp/culture/tourism/post_81.html Takachiho Shrine] (Takachiho Town Office) * [http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/640101.html Takachiho Shrine] (Kokugakuin University) * [https://web.archive.org/web/20120530200534/http://kumaya.jp/atikoti43.html Takachiho Shrine] (Kumaya) * [http://www.komisen.net/index.htm Takachiho Town Community Center (Historical and Folk Museum)] {{Shinto Horizontal}} ==Admission fees== The shrine is open to the public. Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23) | map = {{Infobox mapframe|type=shape|zoom=15|frame-width=200}} }} '''Takachiho Shrine''' (たかちほじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} located in [[Takachiho Town]], [[Nishiusuki District]], {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. It is a notable contender for the national historical shrine "Takachiho-Sume-Gami," though it was classified only as a village shrine under the modern shrine Ranking system. It is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the jurisdiction of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Shrine name == Historically, the shrine was known as "Jussha Daijingu" or "Jussha-no-Miya." In {{ill|1871|en|1871|WD=Q7746|lt=1871}} (4th year of [[Meiji]]), it was renamed "Mitai Shrine," and in {{ill|1895|en|1895|WD=Q7844|lt=1895}} (28th year of Meiji), it was renamed to its current name, Takachiho Shrine. == Deities == The primary deity enshrined is Takachiho-Sume-Gami in the first hall, and Jussha-Daijingu in the second hall. Takachiho-Sume-Gami refers collectively to the ancestral deities of Japanese mythology known as the "Three Generations of Hyuga" and their consorts (Amatsuhikohikohohodemi-no-Mikoto and Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto, Hoori-no-Mikoto and Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto, Hiko-nagisatake-ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto and Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto). Jussha-Daijingu refers to the elder brother of Emperor Jimmu, Mikenu-no-Mikoto, and nine other deities who are his wife and children (Unomehime-no-Mikoto and their children Mikotaro-no-Mikoto, Jiro-no-Mikoto, Saburo-no-Mikoto, Unemi-no-Mikoto, Teruno-no-Mikoto, Otono-no-Mikoto, Reisha-no-Mikoto, Asarabe-no-Mikoto). Mikenu-no-Mikoto, central to Jussha-Daijingu, is said to have crossed to the eternal land after stepping on the waves in the "Kojiki" and "Nihon Shoki," but local legend holds that he returned to Takachiho, vanquished the demon Kihachi, and established his palace here. Another legend in the "Hachiman Usa-gun Otogami-shu" of 1313 claims that Takachiho-Gami is another name for Kami-Yatsui-no-Mikoto, a child of Emperor Jimmu, and the elder brother of the deity enshrined at [[Aso Shrine]]. The "Heike Monogatari" describes Takachiho-Gami as a dragon revered in Hyūga Province. Unomehime-no-Mikoto, according to local legend, was rescued by Mikenu-no-Mikoto from the demon Kihachi and later became his consort. == History == Takachiho is traditionally known as the location of the Takachiho Palace, home to the "Three Generations of Hyuga" deities. The shrine incorporates elements of local beliefs, myths of the descent of deities, and [[Kumano Shugendo]] practices. The {{ill|Kushifuru Shrine|en|Kushifuru Shrine|WD=Q3200650|lt=Kushifuru Shrine}} has historically held autumn festivals in conjunction with the spring festivals of Takachiho Shrine. According to shrine legend, the shrine was established by Mikenu-no-Mikoto, who erected a sacred pole and enshrined the "Three Generations of Hyuga" deities and their consorts. Later, he and nine other deities were enshrined as Jussha-Daijingu. During the reign of Emperor Sujin, the first shrine buildings were constructed. If the shrine is indeed the historical "Takachiho-Gami," it received imperial recognition and Ranks, but it is not listed in the "Engishiki Jinmyōchō." During the mid-{{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, descendants of Mikenu-no-Mikoto served the shrine, and by the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}, it was revered by local lords and the imperial court. The shrine was associated with the Kumano shrines and played a significant role in local politics and religious practices. In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the shrine received 200 koku from the lords of the {{ill|Nobeoka Domain|en|Nobeoka Domain|WD=Q10863441|lt=Nobeoka Domain}}, and it was further supported by the {{ill|Miura|en|Miura|WD=Q347335|lt=Miura}} and [[Naito]] families. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], it was designated as a village shrine and later became a Beppyo Shrine in {{ill|1971|en|1971|WD=Q2475|lt=1971}} (46th year of {{ill|Shōwa|en|Shōwa|WD=Q398996|lt=Shōwa}}). === Ranks === As a historical shrine, it received Ranks such as Jugoi-ge in {{ill|843|en|843|WD=Q23469|lt=843}} and Jushii-jo in {{ill|858|en|858|WD=Q30371|lt=858}}. == ceremony == * **festival (April 16)** - Prayers for a good harvest, with a mikoshi procession to the Otabisho at [[Takamagahara Shrine]], where kagura is performed. * **Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23)** - All 33 dances of the Takachiho Night Kagura, designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property, are performed overnight. Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23) | map = {{Infobox mapframe|type=shape|zoom=15|frame-width=200}} }} '''Takachiho Shrine''' (たかちほじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} located in [[Takachiho Town]], [[Nishiusuki District]], {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. It is a notable contender for the national historical shrine "Takachiho-Sume-Gami," though it was classified only as a village shrine under the modern shrine Ranking system. It is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the jurisdiction of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Shrine name == Historically, the shrine was known as "Jussha Daijingu" or "Jussha-no-Miya." In {{ill|1871|en|1871|WD=Q7746|lt=1871}} (4th year of [[Meiji]]), it was renamed "Mitai Shrine," and in {{ill|1895|en|1895|WD=Q7844|lt=1895}} (28th year of Meiji), it was renamed to its current name, Takachiho Shrine. == Deities == The primary deity enshrined is Takachiho-Sume-Gami in the first hall, and Jussha-Daijingu in the second hall. Takachiho-Sume-Gami refers collectively to the ancestral deities of Japanese mythology known as the "Three Generations of Hyuga" and their consorts (Amatsuhikohikohohodemi-no-Mikoto and Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto, Hoori-no-Mikoto and Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto, Hiko-nagisatake-ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto and Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto). Jussha-Daijingu refers to the elder brother of Emperor Jimmu, Mikenu-no-Mikoto, and nine other deities who are his wife and children (Unomehime-no-Mikoto and their children Mikotaro-no-Mikoto, Jiro-no-Mikoto, Saburo-no-Mikoto, Unemi-no-Mikoto, Teruno-no-Mikoto, Otono-no-Mikoto, Reisha-no-Mikoto, Asarabe-no-Mikoto). Mikenu-no-Mikoto, central to Jussha-Daijingu, is said to have crossed to the eternal land after stepping on the waves in the "Kojiki" and "Nihon Shoki," but local legend holds that he returned to Takachiho, vanquished the demon Kihachi, and established his palace here. The shrine's origin legend, "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki," dated March of the 5th year of Bunji (1189), states that Prince Masakazu, a son of Emperor Jimmu, defeated a demon called Kihachibushi, and later he and his descendants were enshrined as Jussha-Daijingu. Another legend in the "Hachiman Usa-gun Otogami-shu" of 1313 claims that Takachiho-Gami is another name for Kami-Yatsui-no-Mikoto, a child of Emperor Jimmu, and the elder brother of the deity enshrined at [[Aso Shrine]]. The "Heike Monogatari" describes Takachiho-Gami as a dragon revered in Hyūga Province. Unomehime-no-Mikoto, according to local legend, was rescued by Mikenu-no-Mikoto from the demon Kihachi and later became his consort. == History == Takachiho is traditionally known as the location of the Takachiho Palace, home to the "Three Generations of Hyuga" deities. The shrine incorporates elements of local beliefs, myths of the descent of deities, and [[Kumano Shugendo]] practices. The {{ill|Kushifuru Shrine|en|Kushifuru Shrine|WD=Q3200650|lt=Kushifuru Shrine}} has historically held autumn festivals in conjunction with the spring festivals of Takachiho Shrine. According to shrine legend, the shrine was established by Mikenu-no-Mikoto, who erected a sacred pole and enshrined the "Three Generations of Hyuga" deities and their consorts. Later, he and nine other deities were enshrined as Jussha-Daijingu. During the reign of Emperor Sujin, the first shrine buildings were constructed. If the shrine is indeed the historical "Takachiho-Gami," it received imperial recognition and Ranks, but it is not listed in the "Engishiki Jinmyōchō." During the mid-{{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, descendants of Mikenu-no-Mikoto served the shrine, and by the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}, it was revered by local lords and the imperial court. The shrine was associated with the Kumano shrines and played a significant role in local politics and religious practices. In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the shrine received 200 koku from the lords of the {{ill|Nobeoka Domain|en|Nobeoka Domain|WD=Q10863441|lt=Nobeoka Domain}}, and it was further supported by the {{ill|Miura|en|Miura|WD=Q347335|lt=Miura}} and [[Naito]] families. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], it was designated as a village shrine and later became a Beppyo Shrine in {{ill|1971|en|1971|WD=Q2475|lt=1971}} (46th year of {{ill|Shōwa|en|Shōwa|WD=Q398996|lt=Shōwa}}). === Ranks === As a historical shrine, it received Ranks such as Jugoi-ge in {{ill|843|en|843|WD=Q23469|lt=843}} and Jushii-jo in {{ill|858|en|858|WD=Q30371|lt=858}}. == ceremony == * **festival (April 16)** - Prayers for a good harvest, with a mikoshi procession to the Otabisho at [[Takamagahara Shrine]], where kagura is performed. * **Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23)** - All 33 dances of the Takachiho Night Kagura, designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property, are performed overnight. Throughout the year, a selection of four dances is performed for tourists. * **Inoshishi Kake Matsuri (December 3 of the lunar calendar)** - Originally a ritual involving the sacrifice of a 16-year-old virgin to appease the demon Kihachi, it was changed to the offering of wild boars by Kai Munekane, a retainer of the Mitai family. The ceremony includes offerings at the three Kihachi Kofuns and the Sasa Furi ceremony at the shrine, where a whole boar is offered, and the "Onihachinenase Uta" is sung while performing the "Sasa Furi Kagura." === Shrine Priests === According to the "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki," descendants of Jussha-Daijingu served as priests for generations. In 1314, a priest named Sone wrote about his family's long service to the shrine. The "Senmyo" priestly roles were established in the medieval period by the Mitai family, who divided the shrine's territory into ten districts, each served by a "Senmyo" priest. The roles and lineage of these priests remain unclear in later periods. == Shrine Buildings == The main hall is a large Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style building with a copper roof, featuring unique carvings related to local legends and rituals, such as the demon-slaying Mikenuno-no-Mikoto. The shrine is designated as an Important Cultural Property. In 1837, Matsuura Takeshiro described the shrine in his travel journal. == Sub-Shrines == * **Inari Shrine** - A small shrine attached to the east side of the main hall, dedicated to Kotoshironushi-no-Kami and Ootonoshi-no-Kami. * **Aratate Shrine and Shiko Shrine** - Located to the left of the main hall, dedicated to Sarutahiko-no-Mikoto, Amenouzume-no-Mikoto, Emperor Jimmu, and other imperial family members. The original Aratate Shrine was merged into Takachiho Shrine in the late Meiji period but was later reestablished at its original location. * **Other Sub-Shrines** - Gate Guardian deity (deity unknown), Yasaka Shrine (Susanoo-no-Mikoto), Goryo Shrine (Onakatomi-no-Mikoto), Tenjin Shrine (Sugawara-no-Michizane), Hibarino Shrine (Amanootomaro-no-Mikoto), Chinjusha (deity unknown), and the detached Ichi-no Shrine. == Cultural Properties == [[File:Takachiho-jinja, Hon-den 01.jpg|thumb|200px|main hall (Important Cultural Property)]] [[File:Takachiho-jinja, Sculpture Decoration of Hon-den 01.jpg|thumb|200px|Carvings on the main hall
Depicting the slaying of the demon Kihachi by Mikenuno-no-Mikoto.]] === National Important Cultural Property === * **main hall** - Built in 1778 in the early Edo period, featuring Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style with copper roofing, including an Inari shrine. The structure is noted for its detailed carvings and regional characteristics. Designated in 2004. * **Iron Komainu Pair** - Cast iron statues of guardian dogs donated by Minamoto no Yoritomo, designated in 1971. * **Wooden God Statues (2 sitting figures)** - Originally from Aratate Shrine, these statues were moved to Takachiho Shrine. They were designated as Important Cultural Property in 2020. === Takachiho Town Cultural Property === * **Nine God Masks** - Designated as Tangible Cultural Property in 1969. * **Takachiho Shrine Documents** - Designated as Tangible Cultural Property, including the "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki." * **Takachiho Shrine's Father Cedar** - A large cedar tree believed to have been planted by Hatakeyama Shigetada, designated as a Natural Monument in 1969. == Surrounding Historical Sites == * [[Takachiho Gorge]] * **Jussha-Daijingu Ichino-Shomori** - Town-designated historical site located in front of the shrine. * **Kihachi Mounds** - Three Kofuns for the demon Kihachi, located in Kamidono, Tokugenji Temple, and Takachiho High School. Other related sites include "Kihachi's Power Stone" in Takachiho Gorge, "Kihachi's Severed Stone" in Kamiyama, and "Kihachi's Knee Stone" in Take-no-sako. == References == {{Reflist}} == Further Reading == * Kenichi Tanigawa, ed. "Nihon no Kamigami - Shrines and Sacred Places" Volume 1, Kyushu, Hakusuisha, 1984 ISBN 4-560-02211-9 * "Miyazaki Prefecture's Place names" (Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei 46), Heibonsha, 1997 ISBN 4-582-49046-8 * "Udo Shrine and Takachiho Shrine" (Weekly Shrine Travel No. 47), Gakken, 2003 == Related Books == * S. Azu and Y. Umeda, eds., "Shinto Dictionary," Jinja Shinpōsha, 1968, pp. 35-36 * E. Shirai and M. Toki, eds., "Shrine Dictionary," Tōkyōdō Shuppan, 1979, p. 208 * M. Sugata, "Encyclopedia of Japanese Shrines," Nihon Bungeisha, 1989, pp. 238-239 * "The Book of Shinto," Gakken, 1992, p. 226 == See Also == {{Commonscat|Takachiho-jinja}} * {{ill|Kushifuru Shrine|en|Kushifuru Shrine|WD=Q3200650|lt=Kushifuru Shrine}} - Another contender for "Takachiho-Gami" == External Links == * [http://www.town-takachiho.jp/culture/tourism/post_81.html Takachiho Shrine] (Takachiho Town Office) * [http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/640101.html Takachiho Shrine] (Kokugakuin University) * [https://web.archive.org/web/20120530200534/http://kumaya.jp/atikoti43.html Takachiho Shrine] (Kumaya) * [http://www.komisen.net/index.htm Takachiho Town Community Center (Historical and Folk Museum)] {{Shinto Horizontal}} ==Admission fees== The shrine is open to the public. However, an admission fee is payable. *500 yen per person over 20 years old. *400 yen per person under 20 years old. ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Beppyo Shrines}}]] {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{translated page|ja|高千穂神社|version=103557806|comment=Imported full ja history}} [[image:takachihojinja.jpg|thumb|200px|Kagura Hall where nightly performances of Takachiho Night Kagura are held]] [[image:yokagura.jpg|thumb|200px|Night Kagura at the Kagura Hall]] [[en:Takachiho Shrine]] [[ja:高千穂神社]] {{Commons category|Takachiho-jinja}} [[fr:Takachiho-jinja]] [[zh:高千穗神社]] {{Commons category|Takachiho-jinja}} [[fr:Takachiho-jinja]] [[zh:高千穗神社]] {{wikidata link|Q3514126}} [[Category:Architecture of Takachiho Town]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Cultural heritage monuments in Japan]] [[Category:Edo period architecture]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties (buildings)]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:Important Cultural Property of Japan in Miyazaki prefecture]] [[Category:Kokushi genzaisha]] [[Category:Municipal History of Takachiho]] [[Category:Nobeoka Domain]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Hyūga Province]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Miyazaki Prefecture]] [[Category:Son-sha]] [[Category:Son-sha in Miyazaki Prefecture]] [[Category:translated pages with valid en interwikis]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Pages with unclosed square brackets]] [[Category:pages]]

Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23) | map = {{Infobox mapframe|type=shape|zoom=15|frame-width=200}} }} '''Takachiho Shrine''' (たかちほじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} located in [[Takachiho Town]], [[Nishiusuki District]], {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. It is a notable contender for the national historical shrine "Takachiho-Sume-Gami," though it was classified only as a village shrine under the modern shrine Ranking system. It is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the jurisdiction of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Shrine name == Historically, the shrine was known as "Jussha Daijingu" or "Jussha-no-Miya." In {{ill|1871|en|1871|WD=Q7746|lt=1871|1=1871}} (4th year of [[Meiji]]), it was renamed "Mitai Shrine," and in {{ill|1895|en|1895|WD=Q7844|lt=1895|1=1895}} (28th year of Meiji), it was renamed to its current name, Takachiho Shrine. == Deities == The primary deity enshrined is Takachiho-Sume-Gami in the first hall, and Jussha-Daijingu in the second hall. Takachiho-Sume-Gami refers collectively to the ancestral deities of Japanese mythology known as the "Three Generations of Hyuga" and their consorts (Amatsuhikohikohohodemi-no-Mikoto and Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto, Hoori-no-Mikoto and Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto, Hiko-nagisatake-ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto and Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto). Jussha-Daijingu refers to the elder brother of Emperor Jimmu, Mikenu-no-Mikoto, and nine other deities who are his wife and children (Unomehime-no-Mikoto and their children Mikotaro-no-Mikoto, Jiro-no-Mikoto, Saburo-no-Mikoto, Unemi-no-Mikoto, Teruno-no-Mikoto, Otono-no-Mikoto, Reisha-no-Mikoto, Asarabe-no-Mikoto). Mikenu-no-Mikoto, central to Jussha-Daijingu, is said to have crossed to the eternal land after stepping on the waves in the "Kojiki" and "Nihon Shoki," but local legend holds that he returned to Takachiho, vanquished the demon Kihachi, and established his palace here. The shrine's origin legend, "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki," dated March of the 5th year of Bunji (1189), states that Prince Masakazu, a son of Emperor Jimmu, defeated a demon called Kihachibushi, and later he and his descendants were enshrined as Jussha-Daijingu. Another legend in the "Hachiman Usa-gun Otogami-shu" of 1313 claims that Takachiho-Gami is another name for Kami-Yatsui-no-Mikoto, a child of Emperor Jimmu, and the elder brother of the deity enshrined at [[Aso Shrine]]. The "Heike Monogatari" describes Takachiho-Gami as a dragon revered in Hyūga Province. Unomehime-no-Mikoto, according to local legend, was rescued by Mikenu-no-Mikoto from the demon Kihachi and later became his consort. == History == Takachiho is traditionally known as the location of the Takachiho Palace, home to the "Three Generations of Hyuga" deities. The shrine incorporates elements of local beliefs, myths of the descent of deities, and [[Kumano Shugendo]] practices. The {{ill|Kushifuru Shrine|en|Kushifuru Shrine|WD=Q3200650|lt=Kushifuru Shrine|1=Kushifuru Shrine}} has historically held autumn festivals in conjunction with the spring festivals of Takachiho Shrine. According to shrine legend, the shrine was established by Mikenu-no-Mikoto, who erected a sacred pole and enshrined the "Three Generations of Hyuga" deities and their consorts. Later, he and nine other deities were enshrined as Jussha-Daijingu. During the reign of Emperor Sujin, the first shrine buildings were constructed. If the shrine is indeed the historical "Takachiho-Gami," it received imperial recognition and Ranks, but it is not listed in the "Engishiki Jinmyōchō." During the mid-{{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, descendants of Mikenu-no-Mikoto served the shrine, and by the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}, it was revered by local lords and the imperial court. The shrine was associated with the Kumano shrines and played a significant role in local politics and religious practices. In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, the shrine received 200 koku from the lords of the {{ill|Nobeoka Domain|en|Nobeoka Domain|WD=Q10863441|lt=Nobeoka Domain|1=Nobeoka Domain}}, and it was further supported by the {{ill|Miura|en|Miura|WD=Q347335|lt=Miura|1=Miura}} and [[Naito]] families. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], it was designated as a village shrine and later became a Beppyo Shrine in {{ill|1971|en|1971|WD=Q2475|lt=1971|1=1971}} (46th year of {{ill|Shōwa|en|Shōwa|WD=Q398996|lt=Shōwa|1=Shōwa}}). === Ranks === As a historical shrine, it received Ranks such as Jugoi-ge in {{ill|843|en|843|WD=Q23469|lt=843|1=843}} and Jushii-jo in {{ill|858|en|858|WD=Q30371|lt=858|1=858}}. == ceremony == * **festival (April 16)** - Prayers for a good harvest, with a mikoshi procession to the Otabisho at [[Takamagahara Shrine]], where kagura is performed. * **Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23)** - All 33 dances of the Takachiho Night Kagura, designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property, are performed overnight. Throughout the year, a selection of four dances is performed for tourists. * **Inoshishi Kake Matsuri (December 3 of the lunar calendar)** - Originally a ritual involving the sacrifice of a 16-year-old virgin to appease the demon Kihachi, it was changed to the offering of wild boars by Kai Munekane, a retainer of the Mitai family. The ceremony includes offerings at the three Kihachi Kofuns and the Sasa Furi ceremony at the shrine, where a whole boar is offered, and the "Onihachinenase Uta" is sung while performing the "Sasa Furi Kagura." === Shrine Priests === According to the "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki," descendants of Jussha-Daijingu served as priests for generations. In 1314, a priest named Sone wrote about his family's long service to the shrine. The "Senmyo" priestly roles were established in the medieval period by the Mitai family, who divided the shrine's territory into ten districts, each served by a "Senmyo" priest. The roles and lineage of these priests remain unclear in later periods. == Shrine Buildings == The main hall is a large Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style building with a copper roof, featuring unique carvings related to local legends and rituals, such as the demon-slaying Mikenuno-no-Mikoto. The shrine is designated as an Important Cultural Property. In 1837, Matsuura Takeshiro described the shrine in his travel journal. == Sub-Shrines == * **Inari Shrine** - A small shrine attached to the east side of the main hall, dedicated to Kotoshironushi-no-Kami and Ootonoshi-no-Kami. * **Aratate Shrine and Shiko Shrine** - Located to the left of the main hall, dedicated to Sarutahiko-no-Mikoto, Amenouzume-no-Mikoto, Emperor Jimmu, and other imperial family members. The original Aratate Shrine was merged into Takachiho Shrine in the late Meiji period but was later reestablished at its original location. * **Other Sub-Shrines** - Gate Guardian deity (deity unknown), Yasaka Shrine (Susanoo-no-Mikoto), Goryo Shrine (Onakatomi-no-Mikoto), Tenjin Shrine (Sugawara-no-Michizane), Hibarino Shrine (Amanootomaro-no-Mikoto), Chinjusha (deity unknown), and the detached Ichi-no Shrine. == Cultural Properties == [[File:Takachiho-jinja, Hon-den 01.jpg|thumb|200px|main hall (Important Cultural Property)]] [[File:Takachiho-jinja, Sculpture Decoration of Hon-den 01.jpg|thumb|200px|Carvings on the main hall
Depicting the slaying of the demon Kihachi by Mikenuno-no-Mikoto.]] === National Important Cultural Property === * **main hall** - Built in 1778 in the early Edo period, featuring Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style with copper roofing, including an Inari shrine. The structure is noted for its detailed carvings and regional characteristics. Designated in 2004. * **Iron Komainu Pair** - Cast iron statues of guardian dogs donated by Minamoto no Yoritomo, designated in 1971. * **Wooden God Statues (2 sitting figures)** - Originally from Aratate Shrine, these statues were moved to Takachiho Shrine. They were designated as Important Cultural Property in 2020. === Takachiho Town Cultural Property === * **Nine God Masks** - Designated as Tangible Cultural Property in 1969. * **Takachiho Shrine Documents** - Designated as Tangible Cultural Property, including the "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki." * **Takachiho Shrine's Father Cedar** - A large cedar tree believed to have been planted by Hatakeyama Shigetada, designated as a Natural Monument in 1969. == Surrounding Historical Sites == * [[Takachiho Gorge]] * **Jussha-Daijingu Ichino-Shomori** - Town-designated historical site located in front of the shrine. * **Kihachi Mounds** - Three Kofuns for the demon Kihachi, located in Kamidono, Tokugenji Temple, and Takachiho High School. Other related sites include "Kihachi's Power Stone" in Takachiho Gorge, "Kihachi's Severed Stone" in Kamiyama, and "Kihachi's Knee Stone" in Take-no-sako. == References == {{Reflist}} == Further Reading == * Kenichi Tanigawa, ed. The shrine's origin legend, "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki," dated March of the 5th year of Bunji (1189), states that Prince Masakazu, a son of Emperor Jimmu, defeated a demon called Kihachibushi, and later he and his descendants were enshrined as Jussha-Daijingu. Another legend in the "Hachiman Usa-gun Otogami-shu" of 1313 claims that Takachiho-Gami is another name for Kami-Yatsui-no-Mikoto, a child of Emperor Jimmu, and the elder brother of the deity enshrined at [[Aso Shrine]]. The "Heike Monogatari" describes Takachiho-Gami as a dragon revered in Hyūga Province. Unomehime-no-Mikoto, according to local legend, was rescued by Mikenu-no-Mikoto from the demon Kihachi and later became his consort. == History == Takachiho is traditionally known as the location of the Takachiho Palace, home to the "Three Generations of Hyuga" deities. The shrine incorporates elements of local beliefs, myths of the descent of deities, and [[Kumano Shugendo]] practices. The {{ill|Kushifuru Shrine|en|Kushifuru Shrine|WD=Q3200650|lt=Kushifuru Shrine|1=Kushifuru Shrine}} has historically held autumn festivals in conjunction with the spring festivals of Takachiho Shrine. According to shrine legend, the shrine was established by Mikenu-no-Mikoto, who erected a sacred pole and enshrined the "Three Generations of Hyuga" deities and their consorts. Later, he and nine other deities were enshrined as Jussha-Daijingu. During the reign of Emperor Sujin, the first shrine buildings were constructed. If the shrine is indeed the historical "Takachiho-Gami," it received imperial recognition and Ranks, but it is not listed in the "Engishiki Jinmyōchō." During the mid-{{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, descendants of Mikenu-no-Mikoto served the shrine, and by the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}, it was revered by local lords and the imperial court. The shrine was associated with the Kumano shrines and played a significant role in local politics and religious practices. In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, the shrine received 200 koku from the lords of the {{ill|Nobeoka Domain|en|Nobeoka Domain|WD=Q10863441|lt=Nobeoka Domain|1=Nobeoka Domain}}, and it was further supported by the {{ill|Miura|en|Miura|WD=Q347335|lt=Miura|1=Miura}} and [[Naito]] families. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], it was designated as a village shrine and later became a Beppyo Shrine in {{ill|1971|en|1971|WD=Q2475|lt=1971|1=1971}} (46th year of {{ill|Shōwa|en|Shōwa|WD=Q398996|lt=Shōwa|1=Shōwa}}). === Ranks === As a historical shrine, it received Ranks such as Jugoi-ge in {{ill|843|en|843|WD=Q23469|lt=843|1=843}} and Jushii-jo in {{ill|858|en|858|WD=Q30371|lt=858|1=858}}. == ceremony == * **festival (April 16)** - Prayers for a good harvest, with a mikoshi procession to the Otabisho at [[Takamagahara Shrine]], where kagura is performed. * **Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23)** - All 33 dances of the Takachiho Night Kagura, designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property, are performed overnight. Throughout the year, a selection of four dances is performed for tourists. * **Inoshishi Kake Matsuri (December 3 of the lunar calendar)** - Originally a ritual involving the sacrifice of a 16-year-old virgin to appease the demon Kihachi, it was changed to the offering of wild boars by Kai Munekane, a retainer of the Mitai family. The ceremony includes offerings at the three Kihachi Kofuns and the Sasa Furi ceremony at the shrine, where a whole boar is offered, and the "Onihachinenase Uta" is sung while performing the "Sasa Furi Kagura." === Shrine Priests === According to the "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki," descendants of Jussha-Daijingu served as priests for generations. In 1314, a priest named Sone wrote about his family's long service to the shrine. The "Senmyo" priestly roles were established in the medieval period by the Mitai family, who divided the shrine's territory into ten districts, each served by a "Senmyo" priest. The roles and lineage of these priests remain unclear in later periods. == Shrine Buildings == The main hall is a large Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style building with a copper roof, featuring unique carvings related to local legends and rituals, such as the demon-slaying Mikenuno-no-Mikoto. The shrine is designated as an Important Cultural Property. In 1837, Matsuura Takeshiro described the shrine in his travel journal. == Sub-Shrines == * **Inari Shrine** - A small shrine attached to the east side of the main hall, dedicated to Kotoshironushi-no-Kami and Ootonoshi-no-Kami. * **Aratate Shrine and Shiko Shrine** - Located to the left of the main hall, dedicated to Sarutahiko-no-Mikoto, Amenouzume-no-Mikoto, Emperor Jimmu, and other imperial family members. The original Aratate Shrine was merged into Takachiho Shrine in the late Meiji period but was later reestablished at its original location. * **Other Sub-Shrines** - Gate Guardian deity (deity unknown), Yasaka Shrine (Susanoo-no-Mikoto), Goryo Shrine (Onakatomi-no-Mikoto), Tenjin Shrine (Sugawara-no-Michizane), Hibarino Shrine (Amanootomaro-no-Mikoto), Chinjusha (deity unknown), and the detached Ichi-no Shrine. == Cultural Properties == [[File:Takachiho-jinja, Hon-den 01.jpg|thumb|200px|main hall (Important Cultural Property)]] [[File:Takachiho-jinja, Sculpture Decoration of Hon-den 01.jpg|thumb|200px|Carvings on the main hall
Depicting the slaying of the demon Kihachi by Mikenuno-no-Mikoto.]] === National Important Cultural Property === * **main hall** - Built in 1778 in the early Edo period, featuring Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style with copper roofing, including an Inari shrine. The structure is noted for its detailed carvings and regional characteristics. Designated in 2004. * **Iron Komainu Pair** - Cast iron statues of guardian dogs donated by Minamoto no Yoritomo, designated in 1971. * **Wooden God Statues (2 sitting figures)** - Originally from Aratate Shrine, these statues were moved to Takachiho Shrine. They were designated as Important Cultural Property in 2020. === Takachiho Town Cultural Property === * **Nine God Masks** - Designated as Tangible Cultural Property in 1969. * **Takachiho Shrine Documents** - Designated as Tangible Cultural Property, including the "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki." * **Takachiho Shrine's Father Cedar** - A large cedar tree believed to have been planted by Hatakeyama Shigetada, designated as a Natural Monument in 1969. == Surrounding Historical Sites == * [[Takachiho Gorge]] * **Jussha-Daijingu Ichino-Shomori** - Town-designated historical site located in front of the shrine. * **Kihachi Mounds** - Three Kofuns for the demon Kihachi, located in Kamidono, Tokugenji Temple, and Takachiho High School. Other related sites include "Kihachi's Power Stone" in Takachiho Gorge, "Kihachi's Severed Stone" in Kamiyama, and "Kihachi's Knee Stone" in Take-no-sako. == References == {{Reflist}} == Further Reading == * Kenichi Tanigawa, ed. "Nihon no Kamigami - Shrines and Sacred Places" Volume 1, Kyushu, Hakusuisha, 1984 ISBN 4-560-02211-9 * "Miyazaki Prefecture's Place names" (Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei 46), Heibonsha, 1997 ISBN 4-582-49046-8 * "Udo Shrine and Takachiho Shrine" (Weekly Shrine Travel No. 47), Gakken, 2003 == Related Books == * S. Azu and Y. Umeda, eds., "Shinto Dictionary," Jinja Shinpōsha, 1968, pp. 35-36 * E. Shirai and M. Toki, eds., "Shrine Dictionary," Tōkyōdō Shuppan, 1979, p. 208 * M. Sugata, "Encyclopedia of Japanese Shrines," Nihon Bungeisha, 1989, pp. 238-239 * "The Book of Shinto," Gakken, 1992, p. 226 == See Also == {{Commonscat|Takachiho-jinja}} * {{ill|Kushifuru Shrine|en|Kushifuru Shrine|WD=Q3200650|lt=Kushifuru Shrine|1=Kushifuru Shrine}} - Another contender for "Takachiho-Gami" == External Links == * [http://www.town-takachiho.jp/culture/tourism/post_81.html Takachiho Shrine] (Takachiho Town Office) * [http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/640101.html Takachiho Shrine] (Kokugakuin University) * [https://web.archive.org/web/20120530200534/http://kumaya.jp/atikoti43.html Takachiho Shrine] (Kumaya) * [http://www.komisen.net/index.htm Takachiho Town Community Center (Historical and Folk Museum)] {{Shinto Horizontal}} ==Admission fees== The shrine is open to the public. Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23) | map = {{Infobox mapframe|type=shape|zoom=15|frame-width=200}} }} '''Takachiho Shrine''' (たかちほじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} located in [[Takachiho Town]], [[Nishiusuki District]], {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. It is a notable contender for the national historical shrine "Takachiho-Sume-Gami," though it was classified only as a village shrine under the modern shrine Ranking system. It is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the jurisdiction of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Shrine name == Historically, the shrine was known as "Jussha Daijingu" or "Jussha-no-Miya." In {{ill|1871|en|1871|WD=Q7746|lt=1871|1=1871}} (4th year of [[Meiji]]), it was renamed "Mitai Shrine," and in {{ill|1895|en|1895|WD=Q7844|lt=1895|1=1895}} (28th year of Meiji), it was renamed to its current name, Takachiho Shrine. == Deities == The primary deity enshrined is Takachiho-Sume-Gami in the first hall, and Jussha-Daijingu in the second hall. {{ill|Nishiusuki District, Miyazaki|en|Nishiusuki District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132448|lt=Nishiusuki District|1=Nishiusuki District, Miyazaki}}
{{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}} 882-1101 | website = {{URL|http://www.town-takachiho.jp/kankou/taka-zi.htm}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = | location = {{ill|Takachiho|WD=Q1350939|1=Takachiho, Miyazaki}} }} {{nihongo|'''Takachiho-jinja'''|高千穂神社|}} is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Takachiho, Miyazaki|en|Takachiho, Miyazaki|WD=Q1350939|lt=Takachiho|1=Takachiho, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. It is dedicated to Takachihosumegami (高千穂皇神) and Jisha Daimyojin (十社大明神) and [[Mikeiri no Mikoto]].{{Cite web |title=Click the english button to switch the page language to english since that is the page I am citing, not the Japanese version |url=https://www.miyazaki-archive.jp/d-museum/mch/kagura/nokatano-movie.html |access-date=2023-11-10 |website=www.miyazaki-archive.jp}} ==Overview== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Takachiho Shrine | image = [[File:たかちほ９.jpg|250px]]
Worship Hall | location = Kamidono 1037, Mitai, Takachiho Town, [[Nishiusuki District]], {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}} | coordinates = {{Coord|32|42|23.2|N|131|18|8.3|E|region:JP-45_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | deity = Takachiho-Sume-Gami
Jussha-Daijingu | Shrine Rank = National Historical Shrine
Former Village Shrine
Beppyo Shrine | established = Unknown | main hall = Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style with copper roof | alternate names = Jussha-Daijingu | Pilgrimage = Takachiho 88 Shrines | festival = {{ill|April 16|en|April 16|WD=Q2519|lt=April 16|1=April 16}} | ceremony = Inoshishi Kake Matsuri (December 3 of the lunar calendar)
Sasa Furi ceremony (December 3 of the lunar calendar)
Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23) | map = {{Infobox mapframe|type=shape|zoom=15|frame-width=200}} }} '''Takachiho Shrine''' (たかちほじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} located in [[Takachiho Town]], [[Nishiusuki District]], {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. It is a notable contender for the national historical shrine "Takachiho-Sume-Gami," though it was classified only as a village shrine under the modern shrine Ranking system. It is now a [[Beppyo Shrine]] under the jurisdiction of the [[Association of Shinto Shrines]]. == Shrine name == Historically, the shrine was known as "Jussha Daijingu" or "Jussha-no-Miya." In {{ill|1871|en|1871|WD=Q7746|lt=1871|1=1871}} (4th year of [[Meiji]]), it was renamed "Mitai Shrine," and in {{ill|1895|en|1895|WD=Q7844|lt=1895|1=1895}} (28th year of Meiji), it was renamed to its current name, Takachiho Shrine. == Deities == The primary deity enshrined is Takachiho-Sume-Gami in the first hall, and Jussha-Daijingu in the second hall. Takachiho-Sume-Gami refers collectively to the ancestral deities of Japanese mythology known as the "Three Generations of Hyuga" and their consorts (Amatsuhikohikohohodemi-no-Mikoto and Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto, Hoori-no-Mikoto and Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto, Hiko-nagisatake-ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto and Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto). Jussha-Daijingu refers to the elder brother of Emperor Jimmu, Mikenu-no-Mikoto, and nine other deities who are his wife and children (Unomehime-no-Mikoto and their children Mikotaro-no-Mikoto, Jiro-no-Mikoto, Saburo-no-Mikoto, Unemi-no-Mikoto, Teruno-no-Mikoto, Otono-no-Mikoto, Reisha-no-Mikoto, Asarabe-no-Mikoto). Mikenu-no-Mikoto, central to Jussha-Daijingu, is said to have crossed to the eternal land after stepping on the waves in the "Kojiki" and "Nihon Shoki," but local legend holds that he returned to Takachiho, vanquished the demon Kihachi, and established his palace here. The shrine's origin legend, "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki," dated March of the 5th year of Bunji (1189), states that Prince Masakazu, a son of Emperor Jimmu, defeated a demon called Kihachibushi, and later he and his descendants were enshrined as Jussha-Daijingu. Another legend in the "Hachiman Usa-gun Otogami-shu" of 1313 claims that Takachiho-Gami is another name for Kami-Yatsui-no-Mikoto, a child of Emperor Jimmu, and the elder brother of the deity enshrined at [[Aso Shrine]]. The "Heike Monogatari" describes Takachiho-Gami as a dragon revered in Hyūga Province. Unomehime-no-Mikoto, according to local legend, was rescued by Mikenu-no-Mikoto from the demon Kihachi and later became his consort. == History == Takachiho is traditionally known as the location of the Takachiho Palace, home to the "Three Generations of Hyuga" deities. The shrine incorporates elements of local beliefs, myths of the descent of deities, and [[Kumano Shugendo]] practices. The {{ill|Kushifuru Shrine|en|Kushifuru Shrine|WD=Q3200650|lt=Kushifuru Shrine|1=Kushifuru Shrine}} has historically held autumn festivals in conjunction with the spring festivals of Takachiho Shrine. According to shrine legend, the shrine was established by Mikenu-no-Mikoto, who erected a sacred pole and enshrined the "Three Generations of Hyuga" deities and their consorts. Later, he and nine other deities were enshrined as Jussha-Daijingu. During the reign of Emperor Sujin, the first shrine buildings were constructed. If the shrine is indeed the historical "Takachiho-Gami," it received imperial recognition and Ranks, but it is not listed in the "Engishiki Jinmyōchō." During the mid-{{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, descendants of Mikenu-no-Mikoto served the shrine, and by the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}, it was revered by local lords and the imperial court. The shrine was associated with the Kumano shrines and played a significant role in local politics and religious practices. In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, the shrine received 200 koku from the lords of the {{ill|Nobeoka Domain|en|Nobeoka Domain|WD=Q10863441|lt=Nobeoka Domain|1=Nobeoka Domain}}, and it was further supported by the {{ill|Miura|en|Miura|WD=Q347335|lt=Miura|1=Miura}} and [[Naito]] families. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], it was designated as a village shrine and later became a Beppyo Shrine in {{ill|1971|en|1971|WD=Q2475|lt=1971|1=1971}} (46th year of {{ill|Shōwa|en|Shōwa|WD=Q398996|lt=Shōwa|1=Shōwa}}). === Ranks === As a historical shrine, it received Ranks such as Jugoi-ge in {{ill|843|en|843|WD=Q23469|lt=843|1=843}} and Jushii-jo in {{ill|858|en|858|WD=Q30371|lt=858|1=858}}. == ceremony == * **festival (April 16)** - Prayers for a good harvest, with a mikoshi procession to the Otabisho at [[Takamagahara Shrine]], where kagura is performed. * **Takachiho Night Kagura festival (November 22-23)** - All 33 dances of the Takachiho Night Kagura, designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property, are performed overnight. Throughout the year, a selection of four dances is performed for tourists. * **Inoshishi Kake Matsuri (December 3 of the lunar calendar)** - Originally a ritual involving the sacrifice of a 16-year-old virgin to appease the demon Kihachi, it was changed to the offering of wild boars by Kai Munekane, a retainer of the Mitai family. The ceremony includes offerings at the three Kihachi Kofuns and the Sasa Furi ceremony at the shrine, where a whole boar is offered, and the "Onihachinenase Uta" is sung while performing the "Sasa Furi Kagura." === Shrine Priests === According to the "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki," descendants of Jussha-Daijingu served as priests for generations. In 1314, a priest named Sone wrote about his family's long service to the shrine. The "Senmyo" priestly roles were established in the medieval period by the Mitai family, who divided the shrine's territory into ten districts, each served by a "Senmyo" priest. The roles and lineage of these priests remain unclear in later periods. == Shrine Buildings == The main hall is a large Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style building with a copper roof, featuring unique carvings related to local legends and rituals, such as the demon-slaying Mikenuno-no-Mikoto. The shrine is designated as an Important Cultural Property. In 1837, Matsuura Takeshiro described the shrine in his travel journal. == Sub-Shrines == * **Inari Shrine** - A small shrine attached to the east side of the main hall, dedicated to Kotoshironushi-no-Kami and Ootonoshi-no-Kami. * **Aratate Shrine and Shiko Shrine** - Located to the left of the main hall, dedicated to Sarutahiko-no-Mikoto, Amenouzume-no-Mikoto, Emperor Jimmu, and other imperial family members. The original Aratate Shrine was merged into Takachiho Shrine in the late Meiji period but was later reestablished at its original location. * **Other Sub-Shrines** - Gate Guardian deity (deity unknown), Yasaka Shrine (Susanoo-no-Mikoto), Goryo Shrine (Onakatomi-no-Mikoto), Tenjin Shrine (Sugawara-no-Michizane), Hibarino Shrine (Amanootomaro-no-Mikoto), Chinjusha (deity unknown), and the detached Ichi-no Shrine. == Cultural Properties == [[File:Takachiho-jinja, Hon-den 01.jpg|thumb|200px|main hall (Important Cultural Property)]] [[File:Takachiho-jinja, Sculpture Decoration of Hon-den 01.jpg|thumb|200px|Carvings on the main hall
Depicting the slaying of the demon Kihachi by Mikenuno-no-Mikoto.]] === National Important Cultural Property === * **main hall** - Built in 1778 in the early Edo period, featuring Gokensha Nagare-zukuri style with copper roofing, including an Inari shrine. The structure is noted for its detailed carvings and regional characteristics. Designated in 2004. * **Iron Komainu Pair** - Cast iron statues of guardian dogs donated by Minamoto no Yoritomo, designated in 1971. * **Wooden God Statues (2 sitting figures)** - Originally from Aratate Shrine, these statues were moved to Takachiho Shrine. They were designated as Important Cultural Property in 2020. === Takachiho Town Cultural Property === * **Nine God Masks** - Designated as Tangible Cultural Property in 1969. * **Takachiho Shrine Documents** - Designated as Tangible Cultural Property, including the "Jussha-Kyokudaijingu-ki." * **Takachiho Shrine's Father Cedar** - A large cedar tree believed to have been planted by Hatakeyama Shigetada, designated as a Natural Monument in 1969. == Surrounding Historical Sites == * [[Takachiho Gorge]] * **Jussha-Daijingu Ichino-Shomori** - Town-designated historical site located in front of the shrine. * **Kihachi Mounds** - Three Kofuns for the demon Kihachi, located in Kamidono, Tokugenji Temple, and Takachiho High School. Other related sites include "Kihachi's Power Stone" in Takachiho Gorge, "Kihachi's Severed Stone" in Kamiyama, and "Kihachi's Knee Stone" in Take-no-sako. == References == {{Reflist}} == Further Reading == * Kenichi Tanigawa, ed. "Nihon no Kamigami - Shrines and Sacred Places" Volume 1, Kyushu, Hakusuisha, 1984 ISBN 4-560-02211-9 * "Miyazaki Prefecture's Place names" (Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei 46), Heibonsha, 1997 ISBN 4-582-49046-8 * "Udo Shrine and Takachiho Shrine" (Weekly Shrine Travel No. 47), Gakken, 2003 == Related Books == * S. Azu and Y. Umeda, eds., "Shinto Dictionary," Jinja Shinpōsha, 1968, pp. 35-36 * E. Shirai and M. Toki, eds., "Shrine Dictionary," Tōkyōdō Shuppan, 1979, p. 208 * M. Sugata, "Encyclopedia of Japanese Shrines," Nihon Bungeisha, 1989, pp. 238-239 * "The Book of Shinto," Gakken, 1992, p. 226 == See Also == {{Commonscat|Takachiho-jinja}} * {{ill|Kushifuru Shrine|en|Kushifuru Shrine|WD=Q3200650|lt=Kushifuru Shrine|1=Kushifuru Shrine}} - Another contender for "Takachiho-Gami" == External Links == * [http://www.town-takachiho.jp/culture/tourism/post_81.html Takachiho Shrine] (Takachiho Town Office) * [http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/640101.html Takachiho Shrine] (Kokugakuin University) * [https://web.archive.org/web/20120530200534/http://kumaya.jp/atikoti43.html Takachiho Shrine] (Kumaya) * [http://www.komisen.net/index.htm Takachiho Town Community Center (Historical and Folk Museum)] {{Shinto Horizontal}} ==Admission fees== The shrine is open to the public.
